chunks: It is but my soul that I discipline with piety,
so that it may come safe on the Day of Great Fear, and remain steady on the sides of the slippery path.
And if I had wished, I could have taken the way leading to the purest of this honey, the finest of this wheat, and the finest weavings of this silk,
but it is far off that my passion should overpower me, and my greed should lead me to choosing the best foods.
Perhaps in the Hijaz or in Yamamah there is someone who has no hope of getting a loaf of bread, nor has he experienced satiety,
or I lie with a satiated belly while around me there are hungry bellies and thirsty livers?
Or should I be as the poet has said:

key_terms.جَوَانِبِ الْمَزْلَقِ: the sides of the slippery path (metaphor for trials or the path to salvation)
key_terms.يَوْمَ الْخَوْفِ الْأَكْبَرِ: the Day of Great Fear (Day of Judgment)

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam Ali choose modesty and self-discipline over luxury?
ai.summary: In this letter to the governor of Basra, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) articulates the principle of *riyadat al-nafs* (disciplining the soul) through voluntary asceticism, ensuring the soul arrives safely on the Day of Judgment. He contrasts his conscious rejection of luxury—despite his ability to choose the finest foods and silks—with the moral imperative of solidarity with the hungry, rejecting the comfort of being 'satiated while others starve.' This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the leader's role as a mirror of the people's condition, prioritizing spiritual purity and social justice over material privilege.
